blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.
**This chapter is examined in every attempt** — eight past-paper parts between May 2024 and May 2026, plus a question in every RTP and almost every MTP.
The dominant form is **reverse working**: you are given two or three leverage figures and asked to rebuild the income statement, or to find sales, contribution, fixed cost, EBIT or EPS from them.

The three formulae are tiny. **The marks are in the profitability statement** that produces them — Sales, less variable cost, Contribution, less fixed cost, EBIT, less interest, EBT, less tax, PAT, less preference dividend, ÷ shares, EPS.

The 2-mark theory parts rotate through a short list: **double edged sword, trading on equity, the range of DOL, and business risk versus financial risk** — asked six times across the MTPs and twice in past papers.

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: **Draw the profitability statement first, every time.** Once it exists, all three leverages are one division each.

concepts.title: 1–2.1 Introduction and the Meaning of Leverage
understand: **Why the chapter exists.** A company faces two kinds of risk. **Business risk** arises from its operations; **financial risk** is the **additional risk a shareholder bears when a company uses debt in addition to equity financing**. ==Companies that **issue more debt instruments would have higher financial risk than companies financed mostly or entirely by equity**.== This chapter measures both.

==**The term leverage represents influence or power.** In financial analysis, **leverage represents the influence of one financial variable over some other related financial variable**.== These financial variables may be **costs, output, sales revenue, earnings before interest and tax, earnings per share** and so on.

==Generally, if we want to calculate the impact of a change in variable X on variable Y, it is termed the **leverage of Y with X**, and is calculated as **Measurement of Leverage = (Change in Y ÷ Y) ÷ (Change in X ÷ X)**.==
That single formula is the whole chapter. Every leverage in it is the **percentage change in an output divided by the percentage change in an input** — only the choice of X and Y changes.
concepts.example: If a 10% rise in sales produces a 60% rise in EBIT, the leverage of EBIT with sales is 6. Nothing more complicated is happening anywhere in this chapter.

provisions.requirement: (Change in Y ÷ Y) ÷ (Change in X ÷ X) — the percentage change in the dependent variable over the percentage change in the independent one.
provisions.exam_angle: Where a question gives two percentage changes, this is the only formula needed.

keywords: influence of one financial variable over some other

memory.trick: Leverage = **percentage out ÷ percentage in**. Choose what goes in and what comes out, and you have named one of the three leverages.
key: Influence of one financial variable over another

concepts.title: 2.2–2.3 The Three Types of Leverage, and Where They Sit in the Profitability Statement
understand: ==**There are three commonly used measures of leverage in financial analysis.** **(i) Operating leverage: the relationship between Sales and EBIT — it indicates business risk.** **(ii) Financial leverage: the relationship between EBIT and EPS — it indicates financial risk.** **(iii) Combined leverage: the relationship between Sales and EPS — it indicates total risk, i.e. both business risk and financial risk.**==
**The chart that makes the chapter easy (§2.3).** Lay out the profitability statement once and the three leverages are simply three brackets down its side:

**Sales** — less variable cost — **Contribution** ⟵ *the top of operating leverage*; less fixed cost — **Operating Profit / EBIT** ⟵ *the bottom of operating leverage and the top of financial leverage*; less interest — **Earnings Before Tax (EBT)**; less tax — **Profit After Tax**; less preference dividend, if any — **Net earnings available to equity shareholders**; ÷ **number of equity shares (N)** — **Earnings per Share**.
==**Operating leverage brackets Contribution to EBIT. Financial leverage brackets EBIT to EPS. Combined leverage brackets the whole statement, Contribution to EPS.**==
So a question that gives you any two of the three leverages, plus one absolute figure, gives you the entire statement — which is exactly how ICAI sets most of the questions in this chapter.
concepts.example: Given contribution ₹12,00,000 and EBIT ₹2,00,000, operating leverage is 6. Given EBIT ₹2,00,000 and EBT ₹1,00,000, financial leverage is 2. Combined leverage is 12 — and the whole statement is already on the page.

official_questions.question: Differentiate between business risk and financial risk.
answer_points: **Business risk** arises from the firm's operations — the composition of its fixed and variable costs and the volatility of its sales. It is measured by **operating leverage, the relationship between Sales and EBIT**, and exists even in a company with no debt at all.

**Financial risk** is the **additional risk a shareholder bears when a company uses debt in addition to equity financing** (SM §1). It is measured by **financial leverage, the relationship between EBIT and EPS**, and arises only from the fixed financial charges — interest and preference dividend.
**Where each sits in the statement:** business risk is created above the EBIT line, by fixed operating costs; financial risk is created below it, by fixed financing costs.

**Who bears it:** business risk is borne by every provider of capital; financial risk is borne by the equity shareholders alone, which is why companies that issue more debt have higher financial risk than those financed mostly or entirely by equity.
**Together** they make total risk, measured by combined leverage, the relationship between Sales and EPS.
official_questions.conclusion: Two marks: define each, then say which leverage measures it.

concepts.title: 3. Operating Leverage
understand: ==**Operating leverage means the tendency of operating income (EBIT) to change disproportionately with a change in sale volume.** This **disproportionate change is caused by operating fixed cost, which does not change with change in sales volume**.==

In other words, operating leverage may be defined as **the employment of an asset with a fixed cost so that enough revenue can be generated to cover all the fixed and variable costs**. ==**The use of assets for which a company pays a fixed cost is called operating leverage.**==
==**Operating leverage is a function of three factors: (i) the amount of fixed cost, (ii) the variable contribution margin, and (iii) the volume of sales.**==

**Why fixed cost is the whole story.** If a firm had no fixed operating cost, contribution and EBIT would be the same figure, so a 10% rise in sales would raise EBIT by exactly 10% — no magnification at all. Every unit of fixed cost that sits between contribution and EBIT is what creates the multiplier.

The study material's own Illustration 2 makes the point with four firms. Firm D has **nil fixed operating cost** and a DOL of **1** — 'there is no magnified effect on the EBIT due to change in sales; a 20 per cent increase in sales has resulted in a 20 per cent increase in EBIT'. Firm A, with fixed costs of ₹60,000 on contribution of ₹70,000, has a DOL of **7**.
concepts.example: Two firms sell the same volume at the same margin. The one that rents its factory has low fixed cost and low operating leverage; the one that owns it has high fixed cost and high operating leverage — and a much sharper fall in EBIT when sales dip.

provisions.requirement: Amount of fixed cost, variable contribution margin, and volume of sales.

official_questions.question: ShirtCo is a garment manufacturing company producing and selling 10,000 shirts every year. The company's cost and revenue structure is given. Calculate the operating leverage, and compute the impact on EBIT if sales rise by 10%.
answer_points: **Statement of profitability.** Sales revenue (10,000 × selling price), less variable cost (10,000 × variable cost per shirt), gives **contribution**; less fixed operating cost gives **EBIT**.

On the study material's own figures for this question type — selling price ₹500, variable cost ₹200, fixed operating cost ₹25,00,000 — sales are ₹50,00,000, variable cost ₹20,00,000, **contribution ₹30,00,000**, and **EBIT ₹5,00,000**.
**Operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹30,00,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 = **6 times**.

**Impact of a 10% rise in sales.** Operating leverage = % change in EBIT ÷ % change in sales, so % change in EBIT = 6 × 10% = **60%**. In money terms, EBIT rises by ₹5,00,000 × 60% = **₹3,00,000**, to ₹8,00,000.
**Comment.** A DOL of 6 means a 1% change in sales moves EBIT by 6% in the same direction — the magnification created entirely by the ₹25,00,000 of fixed operating cost.
official_questions.conclusion: Statement, then one division, then the percentage — and a sentence saying what the number means.

concepts.title: 3.1 The Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2024 Q1(b), Sep 2025 Q2(a), May 2026 Q1(a)) · MTP 3
understand: ==When we measure the magnitude of the disproportionate change, it is termed the **degree** of leverage. **Degree of Operating Leverage may be defined as the percentage change in EBIT with respect to the percentage change in sales quantity**: **DOL = Percentage Change in EBIT ÷ Percentage Change in Sales**.==

**The derivation that gives the working formula.** **EBIT = Q(S − V) − F**, where **Q** is sales quantity, **S** the selling price per unit, **V** the variable cost per unit and **F** the fixed cost. Since **the change in fixed cost is nil**, F drops out of the numerator of the change, leaving ==**DOL = Q(S − V) ÷ [Q(S − V) − F]**==, which is ==**DOL = Contribution ÷ (Contribution − Fixed Cost) = Contribution ÷ EBIT**.==

**The three situations the study material tabulates.** **Situation 1 — no fixed cost:** sales rise 50% and EBIT rises 50%, so **DOL = 1**. **Situation 2 — positive leverage:** with fixed cost of ₹50,000, sales rise 50% and EBIT rises 100%, so **DOL = 2**. **Situation 3 — when EBIT is nil (contribution equals fixed cost):** DOL = Contribution ÷ 0 = **undefined**.
==**When DOL is more than one, operating leverage exists. The more the DOL, the higher the operating leverage.**==

==**A positive DOL means the firm is operating at a higher level than the break-even level, and both sales and EBIT move in the same direction. In the case of a negative DOL, the firm operates at lower than break-even sales and EBIT is negative.**==

**The analysis table.** **No fixed cost → no operating leverage. Higher fixed cost → higher break-even point. Higher than break-even level → positive operating leverage. Lower than break-even level → negative operating leverage.**

==**The range rule, which ICAI has asked directly: DOL can never be between zero and one. It can be zero or less, or it can be one or more.**== The study material explains the shape: **when sales are much higher than break-even sales, DOL will be slightly more than one; with a decrease in sales, DOL will increase; at break-even point, DOL will be infinite; when sales are slightly less than break-even, DOL will be negative infinite; with further reduction in sales, DOL will move towards zero; and at zero sales, DOL will also be zero.**
concepts.example: May 2026 gave one line: a 5% increase in sales raises operating profit by ₹9,000, with a 40% contribution ratio. Since 5% of sales × 40% = ₹9,000, sales are ₹4,50,000 — the whole statement unlocked from a single sentence.

official_questions.question: The finance manager of A Ltd. noticed that a 5% increase in sales leads to an increase of ₹9,000 in operating profit. The company operates with a given contribution ratio and fixed annual operating cost. Determine the current level of sales and prepare the income statement.
answer_points: **Find current sales.** Let present sales be X. A 5% increase in sales raises contribution — and therefore operating profit, fixed cost being unchanged — by **5% of sales × P/V ratio**. So 0.05X × 0.40 = ₹9,000, i.e. **0.02X = ₹9,000** and **current sales (X) = ₹4,50,000**.

**ICAI's alternative route to the same figure.** P/V ratio = change in profit ÷ change in sales, so 0.40 = ₹9,000 ÷ change in sales, giving a change in sales of **₹22,500**; and since that change is 5% of sales, total sales = ₹22,500 ÷ 0.05 = **₹4,50,000**.
**Income statement.** Sales **₹4,50,000**; contribution at 40% = **₹1,80,000**; less fixed annual operating cost **₹1,35,000**; **EBIT = ₹45,000**.
**The leverages then follow.** DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹45,000 = **4 times**; DFL = EBIT ÷ EBT once interest is deducted; DCL = DOL × DFL.
The examinable idea is that **a percentage change in sales and the money change in operating profit are linked only through the P/V ratio**, because fixed cost does not move.
official_questions.conclusion: One sentence of data, one equation, then the whole statement.
keywords: change in profit over change in sales

official_questions.question: M/s KRY Limited's capital structure is: equity share capital (12,500 shares of ₹100 each) ₹12,50,000; 6% debentures ₹50,00,000; 8% bank loan (amount not given). Total sales ₹75,00,000; P/V ratio 40%; operating leverage 2.4; combined leverage 3.84; corporate tax rate 30%; P/E ratio 8. Calculate (i) earnings before interest and tax, (ii) fixed cost excluding interest, (iii) the amount of the bank loan and the bank interest, (iv) earnings per share, (v) market price per share.
answer_points: **(i) EBIT.** Contribution = Sales × P/V ratio = ₹75,00,000 × 40% = **₹30,00,000**. Operating leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT, so **EBIT = ₹30,00,000 ÷ 2.4 = ₹12,50,000**.
**(ii) Fixed cost excluding interest** = Contribution − EBIT = ₹30,00,000 − ₹12,50,000 = **₹17,50,000**.

**(iii) Bank loan and interest.** Combined leverage = DOL × DFL, so **DFL = 3.84 ÷ 2.4 = 1.6**. DFL = EBIT ÷ EBT, so **EBT = ₹12,50,000 ÷ 1.6 = ₹7,81,250**, and **total interest = ₹12,50,000 − ₹7,81,250 = ₹4,68,750**. Debenture interest = 6% of ₹50,00,000 = ₹3,00,000, so **bank interest = ₹1,68,750** and the **bank loan = ₹1,68,750 ÷ 0.08 = ₹21,09,375**.
The chain to remember: **P/V ratio gives contribution, DOL gives EBIT, DCL ÷ DOL gives DFL, DFL gives EBT, and the interest gap gives the loan**.
official_questions.conclusion: Five requirements, one chain, worked strictly downward through the statement.
official_questions.examiner: No examiners' comments have been published for Paper 6.

official_questions.question: What is the range of DOL?
answer_points: **DOL can never be between zero and one. It can be zero or less, or it can be one or more.**
**When sales are much higher than break-even sales, DOL will be slightly more than one.** With a decrease in sales, DOL will increase.
**At break-even point, DOL will be infinite**, because EBIT is nil and the formula Contribution ÷ EBIT has a zero denominator.
**When sales are slightly less than break-even, DOL will be negative infinite.** With a further reduction in sales, DOL will move towards zero.
**At zero sales, DOL will also be zero.**
The same shape applies to the degree of financial leverage, with the financial break-even point in place of the operating break-even point.

concepts.title: 3.2 Break-Even Analysis and Operating Leverage
understand: **Break-even analysis is generally used to study cost-volume-profit analysis.** It is concerned with computing the break-even point. ==**At the break-even point of production level and sales, there will be no profit and loss, i.e. total cost is equal to total sales revenue.**==
==**Break-even point in units = Fixed Cost ÷ Contribution per unit.**== In value terms, **break-even sales = Fixed Cost ÷ P/V ratio**.

**The study material's Example 1.** Product X sells at ₹40 with a variable cost of ₹20, giving a contribution of ₹20 per unit; on 1,000 units, total contribution is ₹20,000 against fixed cost of ₹15,000, so **EBIT is ₹5,000**, break-even is **₹15,000 ÷ ₹20 = 750 units**, and operating leverage is **₹20,000 ÷ ₹5,000 = 4**. Product Y sells at ₹20 with a variable cost of ₹12, giving a contribution of ₹8; total contribution ₹8,000 against fixed cost ₹5,000, so **EBIT is ₹3,000**, break-even is **₹5,000 ÷ ₹8 = 625 units**, and operating leverage is **₹8,000 ÷ ₹3,000 = 2.67**.
==**There is a relationship between leverage and the break-even point; both are used for profit planning.**== The study material tabulates it twice:
==**Leverage and break-even point: a firm with high leverage has a higher break-even point; a firm with low leverage has a lower break-even point.**==
==**Fixed cost and operating leverage: high fixed cost gives a high degree of operating leverage; lower fixed cost gives a lower degree of operating leverage.**==

Read the two tables together and the chain is complete: **more fixed cost → higher break-even point → higher operating leverage → more business risk**. That single chain answers most theory questions in this section.
concepts.example: Product X needs 750 units to break even and has a DOL of 4; Product Y needs only 625 and has a DOL of 2.67. The product with the heavier fixed cost carries both the higher hurdle and the sharper magnification.

answer_points: **Product X.** Contribution per unit = ₹40 − ₹20 = ₹20; total contribution on 1,000 units = ₹20,000; less fixed cost ₹15,000 gives **EBIT of ₹5,000**. Break-even point = ₹15,000 ÷ ₹20 = **750 units**. Operating leverage = ₹20,000 ÷ ₹5,000 = **4**.

**Product Y.** Contribution per unit = ₹20 − ₹12 = ₹8; total contribution = ₹8,000; less fixed cost ₹5,000 gives **EBIT of ₹3,000**. Break-even point = ₹5,000 ÷ ₹8 = **625 units**. Operating leverage = ₹8,000 ÷ ₹3,000 = **2.67**.

**Comment.** There is a relationship between leverage and the break-even point, and both are used for profit planning: **a firm with high leverage has a higher break-even point, and a firm with low leverage a lower one**.

Equally, **high fixed cost gives a high degree of operating leverage and lower fixed cost a lower degree**. Product X, carrying ₹15,000 of fixed cost against Product Y's ₹5,000, therefore shows both the higher break-even point and the higher leverage.
The practical reading: Product X earns more per unit once it clears 750 units, but falls into loss faster if volume slips.

concepts.title: 3.3 Margin of Safety and Operating Leverage
understand: In cost accounting, ==**margin of safety = (Sales − Break-even Sales) ÷ Sales × 100**==. ==**A higher margin of safety indicates lower business risk and higher profit, and vice versa. MOS is inversely related to operating leverage.**==

**The derivation the study material sets out.** Multiply and divide the formula by the P/V ratio: MOS = [(Sales × P/V ratio) − (BEP × P/V ratio)] ÷ (Sales × P/V ratio). Since **Sales × P/V ratio = Contribution** and **BEP × P/V ratio = Fixed Cost**, this becomes **MOS = (Contribution − Fixed Cost) ÷ Contribution = EBIT ÷ Contribution**.
==Since **DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT**, it follows that **Degree of Operating Leverage = 1 ÷ Margin of Safety**.==

**The study material's Example 2.** Sales of 1,000 units at ₹50 = ₹50,000; variable cost at ₹30 = ₹30,000; **contribution ₹20,000**; fixed cost ₹15,000; **EBIT ₹5,000**. Break-even sales = ₹15,000 ÷ 0.40 = **₹37,500**. Margin of safety = (₹50,000 − ₹37,500) ÷ ₹50,000 = **0.25**. Operating leverage = ₹20,000 ÷ ₹5,000 = **4**, and equally **1 ÷ 0.25 = 4**.
==**The relationship table.** If the **margin of safety rises, business risk falls and DOL (1 ÷ MOS) falls**. If the **margin of safety falls, business risk rises and DOL rises**.==
This reciprocal is the single most useful shortcut in the chapter: a question that gives you the margin of safety has given you the degree of operating leverage, and the other way round.
concepts.example: May 2025's Punyakalash Limited gave a margin of safety of 0.40 and a financial leverage of 1.50. The margin of safety alone fixes DOL at 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5, and with DFL the combined leverage follows at 3.75.

official_questions.question: Financial information for 2023-24 of two companies, N Limited and C Limited: equity share capital (₹100 each) ₹10,00,000 and ₹8,00,000; debt ₹5,00,000 at 10% and ₹7,00,000 at 8%; fixed cost ₹3,00,000 and ₹3,36,000; combined leverage 8 and 4.5; financial leverage 2 and 1.5. Calculate (i) contribution for N Ltd. and C Ltd., (ii) margin of safety in per cent for each, (iii) sales of C Ltd.
answer_points: **Step 1 — EBIT from the financial leverage.** Interest for N Ltd. = 10% of ₹5,00,000 = ₹50,000. DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest), so 2 = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − ₹50,000), giving 2 EBIT − ₹1,00,000 = EBIT and **EBIT = ₹1,00,000**, with **EBT = ₹50,000**. For C Ltd., interest = 8% of ₹7,00,000 = ₹56,000; 1.5 = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − ₹56,000) gives 1.5 EBIT − ₹84,000 = EBIT, so **EBIT = ₹1,68,000** and **EBT = ₹1,12,000**.

**Step 2 — (i) Contribution from the combined leverage.** DCL = Contribution ÷ EBT. For N Ltd., 8 = Contribution ÷ ₹50,000, so **contribution = ₹4,00,000**. For C Ltd., 4.5 = Contribution ÷ ₹1,12,000, so **contribution = ₹5,04,000**.
**Step 3 — (ii) Margin of safety.** MOS = EBIT ÷ Contribution. For N Ltd. = ₹1,00,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000 = **25%**. For C Ltd. = ₹1,68,000 ÷ ₹5,04,000 = **33.33%**.

**Step 4 — (iii) Sales of C Ltd.** DOL = DCL ÷ DFL = 4.5 ÷ 1.5 = 3, which is consistent with contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹5,04,000 ÷ ₹1,68,000 = 3. The P/V ratio is found from contribution and fixed cost: contribution ₹5,04,000 less fixed cost ₹3,36,000 confirms EBIT of ₹1,68,000. **Sales = Contribution ÷ P/V ratio**, the P/V ratio being derived from the data given in the question.
The whole question is one chain: **financial leverage gives EBIT, combined leverage gives contribution, and their ratio gives the margin of safety.**
official_questions.conclusion: Three requirements, worked upward from the leverages — no sales figure is needed until the last step.

official_questions.question: The following information is available for Punyakalash Limited: margin of safety 0.40; financial leverage 1.50; debt ₹1,50,000; tax rate 25%; earnings yield 12%; interest rate (post tax) 9%; market price per share given. Compute the missing figures.
answer_points: **Operating leverage from the margin of safety (SM §3.3).** DOL = 1 ÷ MOS = 1 ÷ 0.40 = **2.5 times**.
**Combined leverage.** DCL = DOL × DFL = 2.5 × 1.50 = **3.75 times**.
**Interest.** The post-tax interest rate is 9%, so the pre-tax rate is 9% ÷ (1 − 0.25) = 12%, and **interest = 12% of ₹1,50,000 = ₹18,000**.
**EBIT and EBT.** DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest), so 1.50 = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − ₹18,000), giving 1.5 EBIT − ₹27,000 = EBIT and **EBIT = ₹54,000**, with **EBT = ₹36,000**.
**Contribution.** DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT, so **contribution = 2.5 × ₹54,000 = ₹1,35,000**, and **fixed cost = ₹1,35,000 − ₹54,000 = ₹81,000**.

**Earnings and the share count.** PAT = ₹36,000 × 0.75 = **₹27,000**. Earnings yield = EPS ÷ MPS × 100, so with an earnings yield of 12% the EPS follows from the market price, and the **number of shares = PAT ÷ EPS**.
official_questions.conclusion: The margin of safety is the key that opens the door; everything else is the standard chain.

concepts.title: 4. Financial Leverage
understand: ==**Financial leverage may be defined as 'the use of funds with a fixed cost in order to increase earnings per share'.**== In other words, it is the **use of company funds on which it pays a limited return**. ==**Financial leverage involves the use of funds obtained at a fixed cost in the hope of increasing the return to common stockholders.**==
==**Financial Leverage = Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) ÷ Earnings before tax (EBT)**==, where **EBIT = Sales − (Variable cost + Fixed cost)** and **EBT = EBIT − Interest**.

**The phrase to notice is 'in the hope of'.** Financial leverage is a wager: the company borrows at a fixed rate and keeps whatever the money earns above that rate. If the earnings exceed the cost of the debt the equity shareholders gain; if they fall short, the shareholders lose — which is the subject of §4.3.

**Where it sits.** Operating leverage lives above the EBIT line and is created by fixed *operating* cost. Financial leverage lives below it and is created by fixed *financing* cost — interest and preference dividend. The two are independent: a firm can have high operating leverage and none at all of the financial kind, or the reverse.
concepts.example: A company earning 18% on its assets borrows at 12%. Every rupee of debt adds 6% to the equity holders' return — the 'hope' in the definition, realised.

official_questions.question: A firm has sales of ₹75,00,000, variable cost of ₹42,00,000 and fixed cost of ₹6,00,000, with loan funds on which interest is payable. Which statement is correct: that the return on investment is less than, equal to, or greater than the interest on loan funds, and is the financial leverage favourable?
answer_points: **Compute EBIT.** Contribution = ₹75,00,000 − ₹42,00,000 = ₹33,00,000; less fixed cost ₹6,00,000 gives **EBIT = ₹27,00,000**.
**Compute the return on investment** as EBIT ÷ capital employed, and compare it with the rate of interest on the loan funds.

**The decision rule (SM §4.3).** When **ROI is greater than the interest rate, the leverage is favourable** — the borrowing adds to the return on equity and to EPS. When ROI is less than the interest rate it is unfavourable, and when the two are equal it is neutral.
ICAI's answer to this RTP question is that **the ROI is greater than the interest on loan funds and hence the firm has favourable financial leverage**.
The examinable idea is that the *level* of the financial leverage says nothing about whether it is good; only the comparison of ROI with the interest rate does.
official_questions.conclusion: One comparison decides it: ROI against the interest rate.

concepts.title: 4.1 The Degree of Financial Leverage (DFL)
understand: ==**The degree of financial leverage is the ratio of the percentage increase in earnings per share to the percentage increase in earnings before interest and taxes.** Financial leverage is also defined as **'the ability of a firm to use fixed financial charges to magnify the effect of changes in EBIT on EPS'**.==
**DFL = Percentage change in EPS ÷ Percentage change in EBIT**, i.e. **(ΔEPS ÷ EPS) ÷ (ΔEBIT ÷ EBIT)**.

**The derivation.** **EPS = [(EBIT − I)(1 − t) − D] ÷ Number of shares**, where **t** is the tax rate and **D** the dividend on preference shares, inclusive of dividend tax if any. On simplifying, ==**DFL = EBIT(1 − t) ÷ [(EBIT − Interest)(1 − t) − DP]**==, which is more usefully written as ==**DFL = EBIT ÷ [(EBIT − Interest) − DP ÷ (1 − t)]**.==
==**If the company has not issued preference shares, DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest) = EBIT ÷ PBT.**==

**The three situations.** **Situation 1 — no fixed interest charges:** EBIT rises 50% and EPS rises 50%, so **DFL = 1**. **Situation 2 — positive financial leverage:** with interest of ₹20,000, EBIT rises 50% while EPS rises from ₹4 to ₹6.50, a rise of 62.5%, so **DFL = 62.5% ÷ 50% = 1.25**. **Situation 3 — when EBT is nil (EBIT equals fixed interest):** DFL = EBIT ÷ nil = **undefined**.

==**When DFL is more than one, financial leverage exists; the more the DFL, the higher the financial leverage.** **A positive DFL means the firm is operating at a level higher than the break-even point and EBIT and EPS move in the same direction. A negative DFL indicates the firm is operating at lower than the break-even point and EPS is negative.**==

**The analysis table.** **No fixed financial cost → no financial leverage. Higher fixed financial cost → higher financial leverage. EBIT higher than the financial break-even point → positive financial leverage. EBIT less than the financial break-even point → negative financial leverage.**

==**The range rule mirrors DOL exactly: DFL can never be between zero and one.** **Financial break-even point is the level of EBIT at which earnings per share is zero; if a company has not issued preference shares, the financial break-even point is simply equal to the amount of interest.** When EBIT is much higher than the financial break-even point, DFL will be slightly more than one; with a decrease in EBIT, DFL will increase; at the financial break-even point, DFL will be infinite; when EBIT is slightly less, DFL will be negative infinite; with further reduction, DFL moves towards zero; and at zero EBIT, DFL will also be zero.==

official_questions.question: Alpha Limited: equity share capital 25,000 shares at ₹100 per share; 15% debentures, 10,000 debentures at ₹750 per debenture; sales 50 lakh units at ₹20 per unit; variable cost ₹12.50 per unit; fixed costs ₹175.00 lakh. Due to policy changes and foreign competition, sales may decline by 15–20%; selling price and other costs remain the same; corporate tax 20%. Calculate the decrease in earnings per share, the degree of operating leverage and the degree of financial leverage separately.
answer_points: **Present position.** Sales = 50 lakh units × ₹20 = **₹1,000 lakh**; variable cost = 50 lakh × ₹12.50 = **₹625 lakh**; **contribution = ₹375 lakh**; less fixed cost ₹175 lakh gives **EBIT = ₹200 lakh**.
**Interest** = 15% of (10,000 × ₹750) = 15% of ₹75 lakh = **₹11.25 lakh**, so **EBT = ₹188.75 lakh**, tax at 20% = ₹37.75 lakh, **PAT = ₹151 lakh**, and with 25,000 shares **EPS = ₹604**.
**Degree of operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹375 lakh ÷ ₹200 lakh = **1.875 times**.
**Degree of financial leverage** = EBIT ÷ EBT = ₹200 lakh ÷ ₹188.75 lakh = **1.0596 times**.

**Decrease in EPS if sales decline.** A 15% fall in sales reduces contribution by 15% to ₹318.75 lakh, so EBIT becomes ₹143.75 lakh, EBT ₹132.50 lakh, PAT ₹106 lakh and EPS ₹424 — a fall of about **29.8%**. A 20% fall gives contribution ₹300 lakh, EBIT ₹125 lakh, EBT ₹113.75 lakh, PAT ₹91 lakh and EPS ₹364, a fall of about **39.7%**.
**Cross-check with the combined leverage.** DCL = 1.875 × 1.0596 = **1.9868**, and 15% × 1.9868 = 29.8% — the same answer the long way round, which is the point of the leverages.
official_questions.conclusion: Compute the leverages, then use them to predict the EPS fall — and show that both routes agree.

official_questions.question: If the degree of financial leverage is 5/4, which one of the following will be the interest?
answer_points: **DFL = EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest)** where there is no preference capital (SM §4.1).
Setting this equal to 5/4: 5(EBIT − Interest) = 4 EBIT, so **5 EBIT − 5 Interest = 4 EBIT** and **EBIT = 5 Interest**.
So **the interest is one-fifth of EBIT**, and equivalently **EBT is four-fifths of EBIT**.
Substituting the EBIT figure given in the question gives the interest directly.
The general rule worth carrying into the exam: **for a DFL of n ÷ (n − 1), the interest is EBIT ÷ n**.

official_questions.question: From the following for financial year 2023-24: financial leverage 4, P/V ratio 40%, tax rate 30%, and other data given. Compute the missing figures of the income statement.
answer_points: **Financial leverage of 4** means EBIT ÷ EBT = 4, so **EBT is one-quarter of EBIT** and **interest is three-quarters of EBIT**. Where the interest figure is given, EBIT follows immediately as four-thirds of it.
**P/V ratio of 40%** gives the link to sales: **Contribution = Sales × 0.40**, and **Sales = Contribution ÷ 0.40**.
**Contribution from EBIT.** Contribution = EBIT + fixed cost, so once EBIT and fixed cost are known the contribution — and hence sales — follow.
**Complete the statement downward:** EBT = EBIT ÷ 4; tax at 30%; **PAT = EBT × 0.70**; and EPS = PAT ÷ number of shares.
**Note the degree of operating leverage** implied by the finished statement: DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT, and DCL = DOL × 4.

concepts.title: 4.2 Financial Leverage as 'Trading on Equity'
concepts.evidence: MTP 1 (Mar 2024 Series I) · SM theoretical question
understand: ==**Financial leverage indicates the use of funds with fixed cost — like long-term debts and preference share capital — along with equity share capital, which is known as trading on equity.**==
==**The basic aim of financial leverage is to increase the earnings available to equity shareholders using fixed cost fund.**==

==**A firm is known to have a positive or favourable leverage when its earnings are more than the cost of debt. If earnings are equal to or less than the cost of debt, it will be a negative or unfavourable leverage.**==
==**When the quantity of fixed cost fund is relatively high in comparison to equity capital, it is said that the firm is 'trading on equity'.**==

**Read the last sentence carefully.** The phrase does not mean dealing in shares. It means the company is **trading upon the strength of its equity base** — using the shareholders' funds as the security on which lenders are willing to advance fixed-cost money, and keeping for those shareholders whatever that money earns above its cost.

**The link back to Chapter 5.** The study material introduced the same phrase among the seven principles of capital structure: the use of long-term debt increases EPS if the firm yields a return higher than the cost of debt, and the leverage impact of debt is greater than that of preference capital because interest is tax-deductible.

concepts.title: 4.3 Financial Leverage as a 'Double Edged Sword'
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Jan 2026 Q3(b)) · MTP 2 (May 2025 Series I, Sep 2024 Series II)
understand: ==**When the cost of 'fixed cost fund' is less than the return on investment, financial leverage will help to increase return on equity and EPS.** The firm will **also benefit from the saving of tax on interest on debts**.==

==**However, when the cost of debt is more than the return, it will affect return on equity and EPS unfavourably, and as a result the firm can be under financial distress. Therefore, financial leverage is also known as a 'double edged sword'.**==

**The three-line rule the study material tabulates for the effect on EPS and return on equity:** ==**When ROI > Interest — Favourable — Advantage. When ROI < Interest — Unfavourable — Disadvantage. When ROI = Interest — Neutral — Neither advantage nor disadvantage.**==

Note that this table differs slightly from the one in §4.2, which grouped 'equal to' with unfavourable. Here the study material calls equality **neutral — neither advantage nor disadvantage**. In an answer, quote whichever table the question's wording points to; the safest course is to say that at equality the leverage adds nothing either way.

**Why 'double edged'.** The same fixed interest that magnifies a good year magnifies a bad one. A company with no debt cannot be pushed into distress by a fall in EBIT; a company with heavy interest can. The sword cuts in whichever direction earnings happen to move.

**The range note that belongs with it.** ==**DFL can never be between zero and one. It can be zero or less, or it can be one or more.**== And the financial break-even point — the level of EBIT at which earnings per share is zero — is where the blade turns: **above it the leverage is positive, below it negative**.
concepts.example: Borrow at 12% and earn 18%: EPS rises, and the taxman funds part of the interest. Earn 8% on the same borrowing and EPS falls, the interest is still payable in full, and financial distress begins.

official_questions.question: Explain in what ways financial leverage operates as a "double edged sword".
answer_points: **When the cost of 'fixed cost fund' is less than the return on investment, financial leverage will help to increase return on equity and EPS.** The firm will also benefit from the saving of tax on interest on debts.

**However, when the cost of debt is more than the return, it will affect return of equity and EPS unfavourably, and as a result the firm can be under financial distress.** Therefore, financial leverage is also known as a double edged sword.

**Effect on EPS and return on equity:** when **ROI is greater than interest** the position is **favourable — an advantage**; when **ROI is less than interest** it is **unfavourable — a disadvantage**; and when **ROI equals interest** the position is **neutral — neither advantage nor disadvantage**.
The reason the same instrument cuts both ways is that the interest charge is fixed: it does not fall when earnings fall, so it magnifies a decline in EBIT exactly as it magnifies a rise.

concepts.title: 5–5.1 Combined Leverage and the Degree of Combined Leverage
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (Sep 2024 Q1(a), Jan 2025 Q1(b), May 2025 Q1(c)) · RTP 4 · MTP 7
understand: ==**Combined leverage may be defined as the potential use of fixed costs, both operating and financial, which magnifies the effect of sales volume change on the earning per share of the firm.**==

==**Combined Leverage (CL) = Operating Leverage (OL) × Financial Leverage (FL) = (Contribution ÷ EBIT) × (EBIT ÷ EBT) = Contribution ÷ EBT.**== The EBIT cancels, which is why the combined leverage can be read straight off the statement as **contribution over earnings before tax**.
==**Degree of combined leverage is the ratio of the percentage change in earnings per share to the percentage change in sales. It indicates the effect that changes in sales will have on EPS.**==

**DCL = DOL × DFL = (% change in EBIT ÷ % change in sales) × (% change in EPS ÷ % change in EBIT) = % change in EPS ÷ % change in sales.** ==**Like operating leverage and financial leverage, combined leverage can also be positive and negative.**==

**The study material's Illustration 3, worked end to end.** Sales at ₹100 per unit ₹24,00,000; variable cost 50%; fixed cost ₹10,00,000; borrowings ₹10,00,000 at 10%; equity share capital ₹10,00,000 of ₹100 each; tax 50%.

Sales ₹24,00,000 less variable cost ₹12,00,000 gives **contribution ₹12,00,000**; less fixed cost ₹10,00,000 gives **EBIT ₹2,00,000**; less interest ₹1,00,000 gives **EBT ₹1,00,000**; less tax ₹50,000 gives **EAT ₹50,000**; on 10,000 shares, **EPS is ₹5**.

So **operating leverage = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = 6 times**; **financial leverage = ₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 2 times**; and **combined leverage = 6 × 2 = 12 times**. ==The return on investment, computed here as return on equity — **earnings after tax less preference dividend, over equity shareholders' funds** — is ₹50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 × 100 = **5%**.==

**Using the leverage to forecast.** If sales increase by ₹6,00,000, that is a **25% rise**. Operating leverage of 6 means EBIT rises by **6 × 25% = 150%**, i.e. by ₹2,00,000 × 1.5 = ₹3,00,000, giving a **new EBIT of ₹5,00,000**. That is what the leverages are for: one multiplication replaces a whole restated statement.
concepts.example: A DCL of 12 means a 1% change in sales swings EPS by 12%. On a 10% fall in sales, EPS is more than wiped out — which is the number a finance director actually needs to know.

official_questions.question: Balance Sheet of EXIM Ltd. as on 31st March 2024: equity share capital of ₹100 each ₹20,00,000; retained earnings ₹4,00,000; 12.5% debentures ₹40,00,000; current liabilities ₹16,00,000; fixed assets ₹50,00,000; current assets ₹30,00,000 — total ₹80,00,000. Fixed costs per annum (exclusive of interest) ₹16,00,000; variable operating cost ratio 70%; total assets turnover ratio 2.5; income tax rate 30%. Calculate (i) earnings per share, (ii) operating leverage, (iii) financial leverage, (iv) combined leverage.
answer_points: **Step 1 — Sales.** Total assets turnover ratio 2.5 on total assets of ₹80,00,000 gives **Sales = ₹2,00,00,000**.

**Step 2 — The statement.** Variable operating cost at 70% of sales = ₹1,40,00,000, so **contribution = ₹60,00,000**; less fixed costs ₹16,00,000 gives **EBIT = ₹44,00,000**; less interest of 12.5% on ₹40,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 gives **EBT = ₹39,00,000**; less tax at 30% = ₹11,70,000 gives **PAT = ₹27,30,000**.
**(ii) Operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹44,00,000 = **1.36 times**.
**(iii) Financial leverage** = EBIT ÷ EBT = ₹44,00,000 ÷ ₹39,00,000 = **1.13 times**.
**(iv) Combined leverage** = DOL × DFL = 1.36 × 1.13 = **1.54 times**, which cross-checks as Contribution ÷ EBT = ₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹39,00,000 = 1.54.
The marks are split 2 + 1 + 1 + 1, and the two-mark item is the EPS — which requires the whole statement, so build it first.
official_questions.conclusion: Turnover ratio gives sales; sales gives the statement; the statement gives all four answers.

official_questions.question: Following information relates to A Ltd. for the year ended 31st March 2025: profit volume ratio 24%; operating leverage 2.00; financial leverage 1.50; and other data given. Prepare the income statement, calculate EPS, and calculate the percentage change asked for.
answer_points: **Work upward from the leverages.** Financial leverage of 1.50 means **EBIT ÷ EBT = 1.5**, so EBT is two-thirds of EBIT and **interest is one-third of EBIT**. Operating leverage of 2.00 means **Contribution ÷ EBIT = 2**, so contribution is twice EBIT and **fixed cost equals EBIT**.
**Sales from the P/V ratio.** Contribution = Sales × 24%, so **Sales = Contribution ÷ 0.24**.
**Combined leverage** = 2.00 × 1.50 = **3.00 times**, meaning a 1% change in sales moves EPS by 3%.

**The income statement** then reads: Sales; less variable cost (76% of sales); Contribution; less fixed cost; EBIT; less interest; EBT; less tax; PAT; divided by the number of equity shares to give **EPS**.
**Percentage change in EPS** for any stated change in sales = the combined leverage × that percentage change.
The habit worth forming: **every leverage given is a ratio between two adjacent lines of the statement**, so two leverages plus one absolute figure fill in the whole thing.
official_questions.conclusion: Two leverages and a P/V ratio are enough to reconstruct the entire statement.

Where the **operating leverage** is given, **Contribution = EBIT × DOL**, and **fixed cost = Contribution − EBIT**.
Where the **combined leverage** is given instead of one of the others, use **DOL = DCL ÷ DFL**.
**Sales** follow from contribution and the P/V ratio or the variable cost ratio, whichever the question supplies.

official_questions.question: Sunrise Foods Limited, a mid-sized packaged-foods company, is reviewing its cost structure and capital mix. Its balance sheet as on 31 March 2026 shows equity share capital of ₹12 crore (1.20 crore shares of ₹10 each), reserves and surplus ₹3 crore, 12% debentures ₹25 crore and current liabilities ₹10 crore, against net fixed assets of ₹32 crore and current assets of ₹18 crore — ₹50 crore in all. Fixed costs per annum excluding interest are ₹10 crore, the variable operating cost ratio is 60%, the total assets turnover ratio is 3 and the income-tax rate is 30%. CALCULATE and comment on (i) earnings per share, (ii) operating leverage, (iii) financial leverage and (iv) combined leverage.
answer_points: ==**Get to sales from the turnover ratio first — nothing else can be computed until you do.** Total assets = ₹50 crore, and total assets turnover = Sales ÷ Total assets = 3, so **Sales = 50 × 3 = ₹150 crore**.==

==**Build the statement down to EAT.** Sales ₹150 crore; less variable operating cost at 60% ₹90 crore; **contribution ₹60 crore**; less fixed cost other than interest ₹10 crore; **EBIT ₹50 crore**; less interest on debentures 12% × ₹25 crore = ₹3 crore; **EBT ₹47 crore**; less tax at 30% ₹14.10 crore; **EAT ₹32.90 crore**.==
==**(i) Earnings per share.** ₹32.90 crore ÷ 1.20 crore shares = **₹27.42**.==

==**(ii) Operating leverage.** Contribution ÷ EBIT = 60 ÷ 50 = **1.20**. A DOL of 1.20 shows fixed costs form a **modest** part of Sunrise Foods' cost structure: a 1% change in sales changes EBIT by about 1.20%, so operating profit is only mildly sensitive to swings in volume.==

==**(iii) Financial leverage.** EBIT ÷ EBT = 50 ÷ 47 = **1.06**. The interest burden is small relative to operating profit — the ₹3 crore debenture obligation is covered nearly seventeen times by EBIT — so the company is financially comfortable.==
==**(iv) Combined leverage.** DOL × DFL = 1.20 × 1.06 = **1.28**. A 1% change in sales moves pre-tax profit and EPS by about 1.28%.==

**What the set of four says about the company, which is the 'comment' half of the question.** Both leverages are low, so Sunrise Foods carries **little business risk and little financial risk** — earnings will not collapse if sales fall. The other side of the same fact is that it has **little gearing to work with**: a recovery in sales will not lift EPS sharply either. A company with a DCL of 1.28 is safe and unexciting, and if the board wants EPS growth it must either take on more fixed cost to buy scale or borrow more to buy the tax shield — deliberately, and knowing it is buying risk.

**The structural check worth stating.** Note that capital employed is ₹40 crore (12 + 3 + 25) while total assets are ₹50 crore; the ₹10 crore difference is the current liabilities. The turnover ratio in this question is on **total assets**, not on capital employed, and taking the wrong base gives sales of ₹120 crore and wrecks every figure after it.
official_questions.conclusion: EPS ₹27.42; DOL 1.20; DFL 1.06; DCL 1.28. Sunrise Foods carries modest fixed operating costs and a small interest burden, so a 1% movement in sales moves its EPS by only about 1.28% — a low-risk structure that also offers the shareholders little leverage on a recovery.

The question says total assets turnover, and the error carries through every line of the answer. The second is deducting interest before fixed cost, which makes the contribution and the DOL wrong even where the final EAT comes out right.

answer_points: **Statement.** Sales ₹24,00,000; less variable cost ₹12,00,000; **contribution ₹12,00,000**; less fixed cost ₹10,00,000; **EBIT ₹2,00,000**; less interest ₹1,00,000; **EBT ₹1,00,000**; less tax at 50% ₹50,000; **EAT ₹50,000**. Number of equity shares = 10,000, so **EPS = ₹5**.
**(a) Operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = **6 times**.
**(b) Financial leverage** = EBIT ÷ EBT = ₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = **2 times**.
**(c) Combined leverage** = OL × FL = 6 × 2 = **12 times**.
**(d) Return on investment** = ₹50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 × 100 = **5%**. Here ROI is calculated as return on equity, i.e. earnings after tax less preference dividend over equity shareholders' funds.

**(e) New EBIT.** An increase of ₹6,00,000 on sales of ₹24,00,000 is a **25% rise**. Operating leverage of 6 gives a change in EBIT of 6 × 25% = **150%**, so the increase in EBIT is ₹2,00,000 × 1.5 = ₹3,00,000 and the **new EBIT is ₹5,00,000**.

mcqs.question: Combined leverage can be read directly off the profitability statement as:
mcqs.explanation: SM §5: CL = OL × FL = (Contribution ÷ EBIT) × (EBIT ÷ EBT) = Contribution ÷ EBT; the EBIT cancels.

why_wrong.D: Tax is applied after the leverages are measured.

mcqs.trap: The cancellation of EBIT is what makes the combined leverage a single division.

mcqs.question: A firm has an operating leverage of 6 and a financial leverage of 2. If sales rise by 25%, EPS will rise by:
mcqs.explanation: DCL = DOL × DFL = 6 × 2 = 12; the degree of combined leverage is the ratio of the percentage change in EPS to the percentage change in sales, so EPS rises by 12 × 25% = 300%.

why_wrong.A: That adds the leverages instead of multiplying them.
why_wrong.B: That is the change in EBIT, using the operating leverage alone.
why_wrong.D: That is the change in sales itself.

mcqs.trap: Option B is a genuine intermediate answer — the EBIT change — but the question asks about EPS.

recap: Combined leverage uses both fixed costs to magnify a sales change into an EPS change.
DCL = DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBT.
The degree is the % change in EPS per % change in sales.
One multiplication forecasts EPS from a sales change.

concepts.title: 5.2 Analysis of Combined Leverage — the Four Risk Combinations
understand: ==**Combined leverage measures total risk. It depends on the combination of operating and financial risk.**== The study material sets out four combinations, and the wording of its comments is what ICAI marks.
==**Low DOL with Low DFL — lower total risk. Cannot take advantage of trading on equity.**==
==**High DOL with High DFL — higher total risk. Very risky combination.**==
==**High DOL with Low DFL — moderate total risk. Not a good combination. Lower EBIT due to higher DOL and lower advantage of trading on equity due to low DFL.**==
==**Low DOL with High DFL — moderate total risk. Best combination. Higher financial risk is balanced by lower total business risk.**==

**The logic underneath.** Business risk is largely given by the industry and the cost structure; financial risk is chosen by the board. The sensible order is therefore to **let the business risk decide how much financial risk you can afford**. A firm with stable, low-fixed-cost operations can carry debt safely; a firm already exposed to swings in EBIT should not add interest on top.

**Why 'not a good combination' for high-low.** It is the worst of both worlds in a quiet way: the high operating leverage means EBIT swings about anyway, while the low financial leverage means the firm is not being paid for that risk in the form of a magnified return to equity. It is risk without the compensating advantage of trading on equity.

Note that the two middle combinations carry the **same total risk** — moderate — but opposite verdicts. The study material is not ranking them by risk alone; it is ranking them by **whether the risk taken is being put to work**.
concepts.example: May 2025 gave candidates three of these four rows and asked them to fill in the comment column using only the words 'lower', 'higher' and 'moderate' — then to name the best combination.

provisions.requirement: Low-low: lower total risk, cannot take advantage of trading on equity. High-high: higher total risk, very risky. High-low: moderate, not a good combination. Low-high: moderate, best combination.

official_questions.question: "The total risk of any business is the combination of degree of operating and financial risk." In the light of the above statement, consider the first two columns of the given table and give your comments in the 3rd column, depicting the total risk profile using only the words Lower, Higher and Moderate. Also select the best combination of DOL and DFL. The combinations given are: DOL Low with DFL High; DOL High with DFL Low; DOL High with DFL High.

**DOL High, DFL Low — Moderate total risk. Not a good combination.** Lower EBIT due to higher DOL and lower advantage of trading on equity due to low DFL.
**DOL High, DFL High — Higher total risk. Very risky combination.**

**The best combination is therefore low DOL with high DFL**, because the firm's low business risk gives it the capacity to carry financial risk, and the financial risk is what delivers the advantage of trading on equity to the equity shareholders.
For completeness, the fourth combination the study material gives — **low DOL with low DFL — is lower total risk, but the firm cannot take advantage of trading on equity**.
ICAI's published answer uses exactly these phrases, so they are worth reproducing rather than paraphrasing.

cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Saraswati Textiles Ltd. reads its own statement
facts: Saraswati Textiles Ltd. sold 40,000 units in the year at ₹150 each. Variable cost is ₹90 per unit and fixed operating cost is ₹15,00,000.
The company carries a term loan of ₹50,00,000 at 12% per annum and has 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in issue. The tax rate is 30%.
The marketing head expects sales volume to rise by 20% next year, with no change in the selling price or the cost structure.
A director, looking at the same figures, says that because both leverages are above one the company is already in danger, and proposes repaying the whole loan from a fresh equity issue.
The finance director wants to know how far sales could fall before the company reaches its break-even point.

questions.q: Contribution, EBIT and EBT for the year are respectively:
reasoning: Option C stops at the post-tax figure, which belongs below EBT; no leverage in this chapter uses it. Option B treats sales as contribution, forgetting the variable cost altogether.

questions.q: The degree of operating leverage and the degree of financial leverage are:
reasoning: Option C inverts both ratios — and the study material's own range rule catches the error at once: **DOL and DFL can never be between zero and one**, so any answer below one is wrong on its face.

questions.q: If sales volume rises by 20% as expected, EPS will rise by:
reasoning: **DCL** = DOL × DFL = 2.67 × 3.00 = **8 times**, which cross-checks as Contribution ÷ EBT = ₹24,00,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 8.
The degree of combined leverage is the ratio of the percentage change in EPS to the percentage change in sales, so the change in EPS = 8 × 20% = **160%**.
Option C applies only the operating leverage, giving the change in EBIT (2.67 × 20% = 53.4%) and stopping one line too early. Option D adds the leverages instead of multiplying them.

questions.q: The director's inference that both leverages being above one signals danger is:

options.A: Wrong, because a leverage above one simply means fixed costs exist; the danger depends on whether return on investment exceeds the cost of debt
options.B: Right, since any leverage above one magnifies losses
options.C: Right, because the combined leverage of 8 exceeds the safe limit of 5
options.D: Wrong, because leverages measure profitability, not risk

reasoning: **A leverage of one means no fixed cost of that kind at all**; anything above one simply records that fixed operating or financial costs are present. The study material sets no numerical 'safe limit', so option C invents one.

SM §4.3 supplies the real test: when **ROI exceeds the interest rate the position is favourable**, when it is below the rate unfavourable, and when equal neutral. Here EBIT of ₹9,00,000 on capital employed of ₹60,00,000 is 15%, against a borrowing rate of 12% — so the leverage is currently working for the shareholders.
Option D reverses the chapter's purpose: leverages measure risk precisely, which is why combined leverage is described as measuring total risk.

questions.q: The margin of safety, and therefore the fall in sales the company could absorb before reaching break-even, is:
reasoning: Confirming it the long way: break-even sales = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio = ₹15,00,000 ÷ 0.40 = ₹37,50,000, against actual sales of ₹60,00,000. MOS = (₹60,00,000 − ₹37,50,000) ÷ ₹60,00,000 = **37.5%**.
Option B is the break-even sales expressed as a proportion of actual sales — the complement of the margin of safety, and the distractor that catches most candidates.

cases.trap: Every wrong option here is a real error: inverting a ratio, stopping at EBIT when EPS was asked, reading break-even sales as the margin of safety, or inventing a safe limit the study material does not give.

cases.title: Integrated Case 2 — Working backwards at Girija Foods Ltd.
facts: Girija Foods Ltd. does not give its board a cost sheet. It reports only that its operating leverage is 2.5, its combined leverage is 5.0, its profit volume ratio is 40% and its fixed operating cost is ₹18,00,000.
Interest on its 10% debentures is the only fixed financial charge. Tax is 30% and the company has 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each.
A proposal is on the table to double the debentures to fund an expansion that would leave the operating structure unchanged.
One board member argues that since the operating leverage is fixed by the cost structure, doubling the debt cannot change the company's total risk.
The board also wants the DOL-DFL profile classified against the study material's four combinations, both now and after the proposal.

questions.q: The degree of financial leverage and the face value of the debentures are:
reasoning: **DFL = DCL ÷ DOL** = 5.0 ÷ 2.5 = **2.0 times**. Option B multiplies the two leverages instead of dividing, and option D inverts the result — which the range rule rejects at once, since no DFL can lie between zero and one.

**Build the statement upward from the fixed cost.** DOL of 2.5 means Contribution = 2.5 × EBIT, so fixed cost = Contribution − EBIT = 1.5 × EBIT = ₹18,00,000, giving **EBIT = ₹12,00,000** and **contribution = ₹30,00,000**.
**The debentures** carry 10%, so their face value is ₹6,00,000 ÷ 0.10 = **₹60,00,000**.

The habit worth forming: **every leverage given is a ratio between two adjacent lines of the statement**, so two leverages and one absolute figure are enough to reconstruct the whole thing — and every derived number should be checked back against the leverages that produced it.

questions.q: Sales, and the margin of safety, are:
reasoning: **Margin of safety** = 1 ÷ DOL = 1 ÷ 2.5 = **0.40, or 40%**, which also equals EBIT ÷ Contribution = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹30,00,000.
Option B gives the break-even sales ratio instead; option C mistakes contribution for sales.

questions.q: Earnings per share as things stand is:
reasoning: Option C uses the whole PAT as though there were only 1,00,000 shares; option A divides EBIT rather than PAT. Tax enters here and nowhere in the leverages themselves.

questions.q: If the debentures are doubled, the board member's argument that total risk cannot change is:

options.A: Correct, because the operating leverage is unchanged
options.B: Correct, because the combined leverage depends only on sales
options.C: Wrong, because combined leverage measures total risk and depends on the combination of operating and financial risk, so doubling the interest raises DFL and with it DCL
options.D: Wrong, because doubling debt always halves EPS

reasoning: SM §5.2: **combined leverage measures total risk, and it depends on the combination of operating and financial risk.** Holding the operating side constant does not freeze the total.

The arithmetic: interest doubles to ₹12,00,000, so EBT falls to ₹12,00,000 − ₹12,00,000 = nil. **At that point EBT is zero, DFL is undefined and EPS is nil — the company sits exactly at its financial break-even point**, the level of EBIT at which earnings per share is zero.
Option D overstates a real effect into a rule; how far EPS falls depends on the spread between ROI and the interest rate, not on the amount of debt alone.

questions.q: Classified against the study material's four combinations, the company before the proposal is best described as:

options.A: Low DOL with low DFL — lower total risk, unable to take advantage of trading on equity
options.B: High DOL with low DFL — moderate total risk, not a good combination
options.C: Low DOL with high DFL — moderate total risk, the best combination
options.D: High DOL with high DFL — higher total risk, a very risky combination

reasoning: A DOL of 2.5 and a DFL of 2.0 are both materially above one, giving a combined leverage of 5.0: a 1% change in sales moves EPS by 5%. On the study material's scale this is **high with high — higher total risk, a very risky combination**.
The margin of safety of 40% confirms the operating exposure: a 40% fall in sales wipes out EBIT entirely, and the fixed interest of ₹6,00,000 remains payable after it has gone.

Option C describes the **best** combination the study material identifies — low DOL with high DFL, where higher financial risk is balanced by lower total business risk — which is precisely what this company does not have, and why the proposal to double the debentures deserves the board's caution rather than its approval.

cases.trap: Question 1 is deliberately built to show the trap of half-solving a reconstruction: the given leverages are the constraint, and every derived figure must be checked back against them.

mcqs.explanation: SM §4.1: DFL can never be between zero and one; it can be zero or less, or one or more.

options.A: It affects both the lender and the borrower
options.B: The same fixed charge raises EPS when ROI exceeds the interest rate and depresses it when ROI falls below
options.C: It applies to both debt and equity
options.D: It changes both sales and EBIT

mcqs.explanation: SM §4.3: where the cost of fixed cost fund is less than the return on investment it raises return on equity and EPS; where the cost of debt is more than the return it affects them unfavourably and the firm can be under financial distress.

mcqs.question: A company has a DOL of 1.5 and a DFL of 2.0. If sales fall by 10%, EPS will:
mcqs.explanation: DCL = 1.5 × 2.0 = 3; the percentage change in EPS = DCL × the percentage change in sales = 3 × 10% = 30%. The direction follows the sales movement.

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.2: combined leverage measures total risk, and it depends on the combination of operating and financial risk.

mcqs.explanation: SM §5.2: low DOL with high DFL gives moderate total risk and is the best combination, because higher financial risk is balanced by lower total business risk.

mcqs.question: At a company's break-even point, the degree of operating leverage is:
mcqs.explanation: At break-even, contribution equals fixed cost so EBIT is nil; Contribution ÷ EBIT cannot be computed. Just above break-even the DOL is very large and falls as sales rise.

mcqs.question: 'Trading on equity' means:

options.A: Dealing in the company's shares on an exchange
options.B: Issuing bonus shares to existing holders
options.C: Using fixed cost funds alongside equity share capital to raise the earnings available to equity shareholders

mcqs.explanation: SM §4.2: financial leverage indicates the use of funds with fixed cost — long-term debts and preference share capital — along with equity share capital, which is known as trading on equity.

mcqs.question: A firm has sales of ₹50,00,000, a P/V ratio of 30% and fixed operating cost of ₹9,00,000. Its operating leverage is:

descriptive.question: A firm sells at ₹100 per unit with total sales of ₹24,00,000; variable cost is 50% of sales and fixed cost is ₹10,00,000. It has borrowed ₹10,00,000 at 10% and has equity share capital of ₹10,00,000 in shares of ₹100 each. Tax is 50%. Calculate the operating, financial and combined leverage, the return on investment, and the new EBIT if sales increase by ₹6,00,000.
answer_points: **Profitability statement.** Sales ₹24,00,000; less variable cost ₹12,00,000; **contribution ₹12,00,000**; less fixed cost ₹10,00,000; **EBIT ₹2,00,000**; less interest ₹1,00,000; **EBT ₹1,00,000**; less tax at 50% ₹50,000; **earnings after tax ₹50,000**. Shares = 10,000, so **EPS ₹5**.
**Operating leverage** = Contribution ÷ EBIT = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = **6 times**.
**Financial leverage** = EBIT ÷ EBT = ₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = **2 times**.
**Combined leverage** = 6 × 2 = **12 times**, which cross-checks as Contribution ÷ EBT = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000.
**Return on investment** = earnings after tax less preference dividend, over equity shareholders' funds = ₹50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 × 100 = **5%**.
**New EBIT.** ₹6,00,000 on ₹24,00,000 is a 25% rise in sales; with an operating leverage of 6 the change in EBIT is 6 × 25% = 150%, i.e. ₹3,00,000, so the **new EBIT is ₹5,00,000**.

descriptive.question: A company has a profit volume ratio of 25%, an operating leverage of 4 and a financial leverage of 1.5. Fixed operating cost is ₹12,00,000 and tax is 30%. There are 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. Prepare the income statement and compute EPS and the combined leverage.
answer_points: **Work up from the leverages.** DOL of 4 means Contribution = 4 × EBIT, so fixed cost = 3 × EBIT = ₹12,00,000 and **EBIT = ₹4,00,000**, giving **contribution = ₹16,00,000**.
**Sales** = Contribution ÷ P/V ratio = ₹16,00,000 ÷ 0.25 = **₹64,00,000**; variable cost is the balance, ₹48,00,000.

**Income statement:** Sales ₹64,00,000; variable cost ₹48,00,000; contribution ₹16,00,000; fixed cost ₹12,00,000; EBIT ₹4,00,000; interest ₹1,33,333; EBT ₹2,66,667; tax at 30% ₹80,000; **PAT ₹1,86,667**.
**Combined leverage** = 4 × 1.5 = **6 times**, so a 1% change in sales changes EPS by 6%. Cross-check: Contribution ÷ EBT = ₹16,00,000 ÷ ₹2,66,667 = 6.

descriptive.question: Two companies operate in the same industry. Company X has fixed operating cost of ₹20,00,000 and no debt. Company Y has fixed operating cost of ₹5,00,000 and interest of ₹6,00,000. Both report sales of ₹80,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 40%. Compute all three leverages for each, and comment on their risk profiles using the study material's classification.
answer_points: **Company X** carries its risk entirely on the operating side — a **high DOL with a DFL of one**, meaning no fixed financial charge at all. On the study material's scale this is close to the high-DOL, low-DFL box: moderate total risk, but **not a good combination**, because lower EBIT arises from the higher DOL and the firm takes no advantage of trading on equity.

**Company Y** has the lower business risk and has used that capacity to carry debt — the **low DOL with higher DFL** pattern the study material calls the **best combination**, since the higher financial risk is balanced by lower total business risk.

**Margin of safety** confirms it: X's is 1 ÷ 2.67 = 37.5%, Y's is 1 ÷ 1.19 = 84%. Y can absorb a far larger fall in sales before its EBIT disappears, which is what makes its interest burden supportable.

**Conclusion.** Y's total risk, measured by combined leverage, is 1.53 against X's 2.67, so Y is both the less risky and the better structured of the two — a reminder that the amount of debt alone says nothing about total risk.

descriptive.question: Explain the concept of financial leverage as 'trading on equity' and as a 'double edged sword'.
answer_points: **Trading on equity.** Financial leverage indicates the use of funds with fixed cost — like long-term debts and preference share capital — along with equity share capital, which is known as trading on equity. The basic aim is to increase the earnings available to equity shareholders using fixed cost fund.

A firm is known to have a **positive or favourable leverage when its earnings are more than the cost of debt**; if earnings are equal to or less than the cost of debt it will be a negative or unfavourable leverage. When the quantity of fixed cost fund is relatively high in comparison to equity capital, the firm is said to be trading on equity.

**Double edged sword.** When the cost of fixed cost fund is less than the return on investment, financial leverage helps to increase return on equity and EPS, and the firm also benefits from the **saving of tax on interest on debts**.

However, when the cost of debt is more than the return, it affects return on equity and EPS unfavourably, and as a result **the firm can be under financial distress**. That two-way effect is why financial leverage is called a double edged sword.

**The rule in short:** ROI greater than interest — favourable, an advantage; ROI less than interest — unfavourable, a disadvantage; ROI equal to interest — neutral, neither advantage nor disadvantage.
The leverage impact of debt is greater than that of preference share capital, because interest is allowed as a deduction in computing tax while preference dividend is not.

descriptive.question: Distinguish between business risk and financial risk, and explain how each is measured.
answer_points: **Business risk** is the risk attached to the firm's operations — the possibility that EBIT will vary because of the cost structure and the volatility of sales. It arises from the existence of **fixed operating costs**, which do not fall when sales fall.

It is measured by the **degree of operating leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT**, or equivalently the percentage change in EBIT over the percentage change in sales. A high DOL means a small change in sales produces a large change in EBIT.

**Financial risk** is the risk attached to the firm's financing — the possibility that EPS will vary, and in the extreme that the firm cannot meet its fixed financial obligations. It arises from the existence of **fixed financial charges**: interest and preference dividend.

It is measured by the **degree of financial leverage = EBIT ÷ EBT**, or the percentage change in EPS over the percentage change in EBIT. Where a preference dividend is paid it is grossed up by (1 − t) before deduction.
**The two combine.** Combined leverage = DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBT and measures **total risk**, depending on the combination of the two.

**The practical distinction** is that business risk is largely given by the industry and the cost structure, while financial risk is chosen by the board — which is why the study material calls low business risk with high financial risk the best combination, and high with high a very risky one.

descriptive.question: Explain the degree of operating leverage and state its range, its relationship with the margin of safety, and its behaviour near the break-even point.
answer_points: **Degree of operating leverage** is the ratio of the percentage change in operating income, EBIT, to the percentage change in sales. It measures how sensitive operating profit is to a change in volume, and is computed directly as **Contribution ÷ EBIT**.
**Range.** The degree of operating leverage **can never be between zero and one**; it can be zero or less, or one or more. A DOL of exactly one means there are no fixed operating costs at all.

**Relationship with the margin of safety.** The margin of safety is the excess of actual sales over break-even sales, expressed as (Sales − BEP sales) ÷ Sales, and also as EBIT ÷ Contribution. Since DOL is Contribution ÷ EBIT, **MOS = 1 ÷ DOL and DOL = 1 ÷ MOS** — they are exact reciprocals.

**Behaviour near break-even.** At the break-even point contribution equals fixed cost, so EBIT is nil and the ratio cannot be computed. Just above break-even the DOL is extremely large, and it **falls steadily as sales rise further above the break-even point**, because the fixed cost is spread over a larger contribution.

**The practical reading.** A high DOL means high business risk: a small fall in sales produces a magnified fall in EBIT, and the company is operating close to its break-even point with a thin margin of safety.
**Using it.** Multiply the percentage change in sales by the DOL to forecast the percentage change in EBIT — one multiplication in place of a restated statement.

quick.a: Operating leverage, financial leverage and combined leverage.

quick.q: State the range rule for DOL and DFL.
quick.a: Neither can be between zero and one; each can be zero or less, or one or more.

quick.q: What is the relationship between DOL and the margin of safety?
quick.a: They are reciprocals: MOS = 1 ÷ DOL and DOL = 1 ÷ MOS.

quick.q: What is the financial break-even point?
quick.a: The level of EBIT at which earnings per share is zero; above it the financial leverage is positive, below it negative.

quick.q: State the double edged sword rule in three lines.
quick.a: ROI above interest — favourable, an advantage. ROI below interest — unfavourable, a disadvantage. ROI equal to interest — neutral.

quick.q: Name the best combination of DOL and DFL.
quick.a: Low DOL with high DFL — moderate total risk, because higher financial risk is balanced by lower total business risk.

differentiate.q: Degree of leverage vs percentage change

differentiate.q: Break-even point vs margin of safety

points: Leverage = the firm's ability to use fixed cost assets or funds to magnify the return to its owners
Three types: operating, financial and combined
Operating leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT — from fixed operating costs — business risk
Financial leverage = EBIT ÷ EBT — from fixed financial charges — financial risk
Combined leverage = DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBT — total risk
Every leverage stops at EBT; tax never enters the ratio

sections.title: Operating leverage and break-even
points: DOL = % change in EBIT ÷ % change in sales
Break-even units = Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit; break-even sales = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio
MOS = (Sales − BEP sales) ÷ Sales = EBIT ÷ Contribution = 1 ÷ DOL
At break-even, EBIT is nil and DOL is undefined; just above it DOL is very large and falls as sales rise
DOL can never be between zero and one

sections.title: Financial leverage
points: DFL = % change in EPS ÷ % change in EBIT
With preference dividend: DFL = EBIT ÷ [(EBIT − Interest) − DP ÷ (1 − t)]
Financial break-even point = the EBIT at which EPS is zero
Trading on equity: fixed cost funds alongside equity capital, to raise the earnings available to equity shareholders
Favourable when earnings exceed the cost of debt; unfavourable when equal or less
Double edged sword: ROI > interest advantage · ROI < interest disadvantage and possible financial distress · ROI = interest neutral
Interest is tax-deductible, so debt leverages harder than preference capital
